Form Factor C for Container Ships

From Part B, 2.3.2.6 of the IS Code:

Formula

C=d⋅D′Bm2dKG(CBCW)2100LC = \frac{d \cdot D'}{B_m^2} \sqrt{\frac{d}{KG}} \left( \frac{C_B}{C_W} \right)^2 \sqrt{\frac{100}{L}}C=Bm2​d⋅D′​KGd​​(CW​CB​​)2L100​​

Definitions of terms

  • d = mean draught (m)
  • D′ = moulded depth corrected for volumes within the hatch coamings: D′=D+h(2b−BDBD)(2 ΣlHL)D' = D + h \left( \frac{2b - B_D}{B_D} \right) \left( \frac{2\, \Sigma l_H}{L} \right)D′=D+h(BD​2b−BD​​)(L2ΣlH​​)
  • D = moulded depth of the ship (m)
  • B_D = moulded breadth of the ship (m)
  • KG = height of the centre of mass above the baseline, corrected for free-surface effect, and not to be taken as less than d (m)
  • C_B = block coefficient
  • C_W = waterplane coefficient
  • l_H = length of each hatch coaming within L/4 forward and aft of amidships (m)
  • b = mean width of hatch coamings within L/4 forward and aft of amidships (m)
  • h = mean height of hatch coamings within L/4 forward and aft of amidships (m)
  • L = length of the ship (m)
  • B = breadth of the ship at the waterline (m)
  • B_m = breadth of the ship at the waterline at half the mean draught (m)

Purpose:

C accounts for hull form characteristics — draught, depth, beam, fullness (C_B/C_W) and size — that affect resistance to capsizing at large heel angles. It scales the five alternative criteria for containerships > 100 m (e.g. area ≥ 0.016/C m·rad to 40°, GZ ≥ 0.033/C m at 30°, GZmax ≥ 0.042/C m). The shaded volumes in the Code’s figure 2.3-1 represent partial volumes within hatch coamings that contribute righting energy when the ship is on a wave crest.

item.title: Loadline Regulations
item.description:
1. Type A ships - Tankers - ships carrying liquid bulk cargo.
  2. Type B ships - All other type of ships.
    flowchart TD
    Ships -->|One| A[Type A - Tankers ]
    Ships -->|Two| B[Type B - all other types of ships]
    B --> |B-60| C[100< L < 150 - survives one compartment flooding ]
    B --> |B-100| D[100< L <150 - survives two adjacent compartment flooding ]

Oil tankers are permitted to have more Summer freeboard than general cargo ships with a similar LBP. They are considered to be safer ships for the following reasons:

1.They have much smaller deck openings in the main deck. 2.They have greater subdivision, by the additional longitudinal and transverse bulkheads. 3.Their cargo oil has greater buoyancy than grain cargo. 4.They have more pumps to quickly control ingress of water after a bilging incident. 5.Cargo oil has a permeability of about 5% whilst grain cargo has a permeability of 60e65%. The lower permeability will instantly allow less ingress of water following a bilging incident. 6.Oil tankers will have greater GM values. This is particularly true for modern double-skin tankers and wide shallow draft tankers.

    flowchart TD
    A[Start] --> B{Tabular Freeboard}
    B -->|Correction 1| C[Depth Correction]
    B -->|Correction 2| D[Block Coefficient Correction]
    B -->|Correction 3| E[Bow height correction]
    B -->|Correction 4| E[Superstructure correction]
    B -->|Correction 5| E[Sheer correction]
    B -->|Correction 6| E[Strength correction]

item.title: Simpson's Rules Applied to Second Moments of Area of Ship Shapes
item.description:
I_x about the X axis and I_y about the Y axis, valid for any view: plan, transverse section or profile*

1. Convention: set this up first

Draw the view you are looking at. Then fix the axes as follows. The formulas depend only on this convention, so they hold for every view.

  • X axis: the line along which the stations are equally spaced (interval h) and from which every ordinate is measured.
  • Y axis: the line perpendicular to X at station 0. Levers are measured from it.
  • y: ordinate (offset) from the X axis to the edge of the shape at each station.
  • n: lever, the station number counted from the Y axis, so x = n·h.
  • SM: Simpson multiplier.
  • k: number of sides of the X axis on which the shape lies (k = 1 for one side only; k = 2 for a shape symmetrical about X when half ordinates are given).
  • To look at the shape from another direction, rotate the drawing until the stations run along X, then reuse the same formulas.

2. Basic integrals (per strip of width dx)

About X Axis

Strip area dA=y×dxdA = y \times dxdA=y×dx. Its own inertia about its base is dIx=y312×dxdI_x = \frac{y^3}{12} \times dx dIx​=12y3​×dx, and moving it by y2\frac {y}{2}2y​ (parallel axis theorem) adds y×dx×y222 y \times dx \times \frac {y^2}{2^2} y×dx×22y2​. Together:

dIx=(y312+y34)×dx dI_x = (\frac {y^3}{12}+ \frac {y^3}{4})\times dx dIx​=(12y3​+4y3​)×dx

About Y Axis

About the Y axis the strip sits at distance x, so dIy=x2×y×dxdI_y = x^2 \times y \times dxdIy​=x2×y×dx. The strip’s own term y×dx312 y\times \frac {dx^3}{12}y×12dx3​ is negligible as dx → 0 and is dropped. Hence, for k sides:

A=k∫ydx A = k \int y dx A=k∫ydx

Ix=k3∫y3dx I_x = \frac{k}{3} \int y^3 dx Ix​=3k​∫y3dx

Iy=k∫x2ydx I_y = {k} \int x^2 y dx Iy​=k∫x2ydx

3. Simpson’s form

Let c=h3c = \frac {h}{3}c=3h​ for Simpson’s 1st rule (SM = 1, 4, 2, 4, … 4, 1; needs an odd number of ordinates) or c=3h8c = \frac {3h}{8}c=83h​ for the 2nd rule (SM = 1, 3, 3, 2, 3, 3, … 3, 1; needs the number of intervals to be a multiple of 3). With levers in whole intervals (x = n·h):

Quantity Working formula
Area A = k·c·Σ(SM·y) A=k×c×Σ(SM×y) A = k \times c \times \Sigma (SM \times y)A=k×c×Σ(SM×y)

Iy: about the Y axis (station 0) Iy = k·c·h²·Σ(SM·y·n²) Iy=k×c×h2×Σ(SM×y×n2) I_y = k \times c \times h^2 \times \Sigma ( SM \times y \times n^2)Iy​=k×c×h2×Σ(SM×y×n2)
Centroid distance from Y axis x̄ = h·Σ(SM·y·n) / Σ(SM·y) xˉ=h×Σ(SM×y×n)Σ(SM×y)\bar x = h \times \frac {\Sigma (SM \times y \times n)}{ \Sigma (SM \times y)}xˉ=h×Σ(SM×y)Σ(SM×y×n)​

Ix about the centroid (k = 1) Ix,cg = Ix − A·ȳ², with ȳ = ½·Σ(SM·y²) / Σ(SM·y) IxCG=Ix−(A×yˉ2)I_{xCG}= I_x - (A\times \bar y ^2)IxCG​=Ix​−(A×yˉ​2) with yˉ=12×Σ(SM×y2)Σ(SM×y)\bar y = \frac {1}{2} \times \frac{\Sigma (SM \times y^2)}{\Sigma (SM \times y)} yˉ​=21​×Σ(SM×y)Σ(SM×y2)​
Ix about the centroid (k = 2, symmetrical about X) ȳ = 0, so Ix is already the centroidal value

For Simpson’s 1st rule these reduce to:

Ix = (k·h/9)·Σ(SM·y³)

Ix=(k×h9)×Σ(SM×y3) I_x = (k \times \frac{h}{9}) \times \Sigma (SM \times y^3)Ix​=(k×9h​)×Σ(SM×y3)

Iy = (k·h³/3)·Σ(SM·y·n²)

Iy=(k×h39)×Σ(SM××n2) I_y = (k \times \frac {h^3}{9})\times \Sigma ( SM \times \times n ^2)Iy​=(k×9h3​)×Σ(SM××n2)

The levers n already include h, which is why the extra h2h^2h2 ( h3h^3h3overall) appears.

4. Mapping to the view you are looking at

View X axis, stations, y k Ix means Iy means
Plan view (waterplane) X = centreline, stations from aft to forward, y = half-breadth 2 Transverse ITI_TIT​ about the centreline. BMT=IT∇BM_T = \frac {I_T}{\nabla}BMT​=∇IT​​ About the transverse axis at station 0. Shift to the CoF: IL=Iy−A⋅xF2I_L = I_y − A·x_F^2IL​=Iy​−A⋅xF2​. BML=IL∇BM_L = \frac {I_L}{\nabla}BML​=∇IL​​
Transverse section (looking fore/aft) X = vertical centreline, stations = waterlines from the baseline, y = half-breadth 2 Section area about the vertical centreline Section area about the baseline. Shift to the area centroid with x̄
Profile (side view) X = keel line, stations along the length, y = depth 1 Area about the keel line (shift with ȳ) Area about the vertical axis at station 0 (shift with x̄)

Rule of thumb: IxI_xIx​ always uses the cube of the ordinate y3y^3y3. IyI_yIy​ always uses the ordinate times the square of the lever y×n2y \times n^2y×n2.

5. Worked example (plan view, Y axis at the after end)

Waterplane with 5 stations, h = 5 m, half-breadths y = 1, 4, 5, 4, 1 m, k = 2, Simpson’s 1st rule.

Stn n y SM SM·y SM·y·n SM·y·n² y³ SM·y³
0 0 1 1 1 0 0 1 1
1 1 4 4 16 16 16 64 256
2 2 5 2 10 20 40 125 250
3 3 4 4 16 48 144 64 256
4 4 1 1 1 4 16 1 1
Σ 44 88 216 764
  • A = 2·(5/3)·44 = 146.67 m²
  • Ix = (2·5/9)·764 = 848.89 m⁴ (centreline, already centroidal because the shape is symmetrical)
  • x̄ = 5·88/44 = 10.0 m from the Y axis
  • Iy about station 0 = 2·(5³/3)·216 = 18 000 m⁴
  • Iy,cg = 18 000 − 146.67·10.0² = 3 333.33 m⁴

Self-check on a rectangle of length 4h and full breadth 2y (Σ SM·y³ = 12y³): the formula gives Ix = (2h/9)·12y³ = 8hy³/3, which equals the exact (1/12)(2y)³(4h). About the end, Σ(SM·n²) = 64 gives Iy = 128·y·h³/3, also exact. Simpson’s rules are exact here because the integrands are polynomials of degree 3 or lower.

6. Common errors

  • Cubing after applying the multiplier: use SM·y³, not (SM·y)³.
  • Forgetting k when half ordinates are used.
  • Using y² in the Iy column. It is the ordinate to the first power times the lever squared.
  • Dropping the h² (or h³) when the levers are written as station numbers.
  • Quoting Iy about an arbitrary axis as if it were about the centroid or the centre of flotation. Always apply −A·x̄² (or −A·x_F²).
  • Using Simpson’s 1st rule with an even number of ordinates.
